newsitem.title: USA: Clinton reviewing Daschle's abortion compromise.
newsitem.headline: Clinton reviewing Daschle's abortion compromise.

text.p: The White House said Tuesday it was "possible" President Clinton could support a compromise proposal by Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle on banning so-called partial-birth abortions.

Debate on banning the procedure was to begin this week in the Senate when it takes up a bill sponsored by Sen. Rick Santorum, a Pennsylvania Republican, that would allow the procedure only when a woman's life is at risk.
Daschle has drafted a compromise that would include bans on all late-term abortions with exceptions for cases where the woman's life was in danger or where she risked "grievous injury" to her health.

"I think that we are looking very carefully at Sen. Daschle's proposed language and we believe that it's possible for the White House to support that language," White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry said.

He stressed, however, that the White House was "completing a review" of the bill and that a recommendation had not been presented to Clinton, who vetoed legislation last year because it did not allow for exceptions to protect the health of the mother.
Clinton's expected support for the Daschle measure drew fire from leaders of the Southern Baptist Convention.

"We write to beg you to reconsider your continued defence of the killing of living premature babies by the brutal partial birth method," the leaders said in a letter to Clinton, himself a Southern Baptist. "We must also note our dismay that in Congress you are supporting legislative language that would permit virtually all partial birth abortions to continue without restriction."

The procedure, which opponents call partial birth abortion and which can also be referred to as dilation and extraction, involves the partial extraction of the foetus feet-first, the subsesquent suctioning out of the foetal brain and removal of the foetus.

Opponents of the ban have said it hampers women's constitutional right to choose abortion, but even some abortion rights supporters have been swayed by a graphic campaign for the ban on the House floor, including line drawings of a foetus being aborted by this method.
The House voted 295-136 on March 20 to pass the ban.

Douglas Johnson, legislative director of the National Right to Life Committee, said Tuesday that while the Senate is likely to pass the Santorum ban, a veto-proof majority of 67 votes was not assured.

Television advertisements sponsored by the anti-abortion Child Protection Fund were being aimed at seven states where senators were believed to be wavering: Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Louisiana, Nebraska and Wisconsin.
